title: Test fixtures for the HTML generation system
body:
Once the HTML generation system exists, it will need **fixture-based testing** — and fixtures are
not free. They have to be created, kept in step with the templates and data shapes they stand in
for, and pruned when those change. That maintenance is the part usually discovered late.

Worth deciding when it becomes real:

- Where fixtures live, and whether they are generated from `_data/` or hand-authored. Generated
  fixtures cannot drift from the source shapes; hand-authored ones cover cases real data does not.
- Whether a fixture is a governed artifact or a test asset. `test/` is not scanned by the audit, so
  today it would be neither.
- How a schema change invalidates a fixture, and whether that is a check or a convention. The
  generator-over-hand-maintenance pattern used for `catalog.md` and specified for the glossary in
  [PLAN-012](../01-plans/PLAN-012-terminology-system.md) probably applies here too.

Related: [PLAN-003](../01-plans/PLAN-003-dynamic-html-generation/PLAN-003-overview.md) — approved,
not built. Nothing to do until it is.

title: Prioritised search order for agentic knowledge retrieval
body:
The retrieval system needs a **stated order of places to look**, not just a set of places. An agent
answering "how does X work here?" currently has no guidance on what to consult first, and the sources
disagree with each other in predictable ways.

Candidate sources, roughly in the order they were suggested:

- **Developed code** — the only source that is true about what *exists*
- **Plan documentation** — intent, which may describe things never built
- **ADRs** — why a choice was made, and what was rejected
- **Session records** — contemporaneous narrative, including corrections
- **This ideas list** — speculation, explicitly not yet decided
- Also worth placing: `brain/` memories, the generated glossary, `systems.yaml`, `AGENTS.md`

**The ordering principle is the real question.** These sources have different relationships to truth:
code is what is, plans are what was intended, ADRs are why, session records are what happened, ideas
are what might. An agent that reads a plan describing unbuilt work and treats it as reality will be
confidently wrong — which happened in this repository on 2026-09-06, where several `systems.yaml`
entries describe aspiration and `PROMPT-003` now asks whether the file is a live registry or a map.

Worth deciding when this becomes real:

- Does the order vary by question type? "How does X work" and "why is X this way" plausibly want
  different first stops.
- Should a source carry a **confidence or freshness signal** so the agent can weigh disagreement,
  rather than trusting whichever it read first? `brain/` memories already have a `confidence` field;
  nothing else does.
- What resolves a genuine conflict between sources — is code always authoritative, or does an ADR
  postdating the code win?
- Does this belong in `tools/load_context.py`, in `AGENTS.md` as instruction, or both?

Related: `sys-retrieval`, [PLAN-012](../01-plans/PLAN-012-terminology-system.md) for the glossary as
one such source, and `phase-term-01`'s `--system` filter, which adds a retrieval axis this ordering
would need to account for.

title: A skill for mid-session notes updates
body:
A skill that updates the session record mid-session, at a natural pause, rather than leaving it as a
closing task. The practice it automates is established: writing while context is fresh and revising
as work progresses produces a more accurate record than reconstructing at the end.

A **skill**, not a slash command. A skill is invokable by the owner as `/name` *and* by the model
when it notices a documentable moment; a command is user-triggered only. There is no case here for
both, since the skill covers the command's behaviour entirely.

Open: whether the model should ever invoke it unprompted, or only offer. Lives in `.claude/skills/`,
which does not exist yet — this would set the pattern for skills in this repository, and
`phase-tool-02` would later want it generalised for other repositories.

title: Vector databases, agentic RAG, and semantic plus deterministic search
body:
Three related ideas, recorded together because they are already scoped in the backlog and the
overlap is the useful information — not a reason to omit them.

- **Vector databases** — `phase-mem-15` (provider, privacy, cost, dimensions, storage) and
  `phase-mem-16` (embedding schema, model identity, content hashes, invalidation).
- **Agentic RAG** — `phase-mem-18` (vector as a measured fallback) and `phase-mem-19` (bounded query
  decomposition and retries with cost reporting).
- **Semantic and deterministic search together** — `phase-mem-18` already specifies vector fallback
  *after* exact, tag and keyword retrieval, which is that layering.

All five are `deferred`. `phase-mem-15` requires **recorded retrieval failures** before choosing a
provider, and `phase-mem-19` requires evidence that refinement would address remaining failures. So
the gate on un-deferring is evidence of retrieval failing, which nothing currently collects.

Worth deciding: what records a retrieval failure, and where. Related to entry `000002`, which is
arguably the conceptual parent — an ordering principle has to exist before you can say a retrieval
missed.

title: Graph databases and GitNexus
body:
Investigate graph-based code and knowledge retrieval. Genuinely uncovered — the whole `phase-mem-*`
line is vector-based.

**GitNexus** (MIT, [github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus))
parses a repository into a knowledge graph entirely client-side: functions, classes and imports
mapped with D3, an embedded **KuzuDB** graph database, a built-in Graph RAG agent, and exposure to
Claude Code and other assistants over MCP. It argues explicitly for Cypher queries over real code
relationships *instead of* vector embeddings.

Complementary rather than competing, most likely: graph RAG answers questions about **code
structure**, vector search answers questions about **knowledge memories**. Worth testing that
assumption rather than assuming it.

Worth deciding: whether to adopt GitNexus as a tool, build graph retrieval into this system, or
both — very different costs. Whether KuzuDB alongside DuckDB is one embedded database too many. And
whether a graph view of `_data/` and `brain/` would answer questions the projection cannot.

title: Audit index widths before they run out
body:
The ideas list moved to six digits before it had a third entry. Other indexes in this system are
narrower and were not chosen with a horizon in mind.

**Document codes are three digits.** `schemas/document.schema.json` pins the pattern to
`^[A-Z]+-(?:[0-9]{3}(?:\.[0-9]{2})?|[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2})$` — so `PLAN-999` is the
ceiling per series, sub-codes are capped at `.99`, and dated codes allow only 99 sessions per day.
`GOV-005` says codes are never reused, so retirements consume the space permanently.

Worth auditing: every index in the system against a realistic horizon for reaching a fully
functioning version — document codes per series, sub-codes, dated session sequences, phase numbers
within a track, and anything in `_data/`. Widening a pattern later is cheap; renumbering issued codes
is forbidden by `GOV-005`, so the cost of being wrong is asymmetric.

title: An agent for triaging parked ideas
body:
An agent whose sole purpose is working this list: triaging entries, scouting the repository for plans
and documentation already related to them, and proposing priority.

This is the process that makes recording ideas as given safe. Overlap between an idea and existing
work is real information, but detecting it should not be a gate at the point of capture — it belongs
to a pass that runs over the list afterward, exactly as `ADR-007` routes ambiguity in captured notes
rather than interrupting for it.

Worth deciding: whether it proposes status changes or applies them; whether it may write `promoted`
entries into the backlog or only recommend; how it reports an overlap it finds; and whether it runs
on a schedule or on demand.

title: Metrics and analysis over the ideas data
body:
The append-only list with statuses is a dataset, not just a notepad. Because entries are never
deleted and every one ends in a status, it records what was considered, what was promoted, what was
discarded and how long each took.

Worth deriving later: rate of ideas per session or per week, promotion versus discard ratio, time
from `open` to resolution, which areas of the system generate the most ideas, and how many
duplicates arise before triage catches them. Candidate for charts, and for a presentation.

This is a reason to keep the data clean at the source rather than a reason to add fields now — an
entry needs a date, a status and a stable ID, all of which it already has.

title: Independent transcript analysis with adversarial session review
body:
An agent that reads the session transcript **directly**, as an independent third party, and writes
its own session documentation. Then run an adversarial review between that record and the one the
working agent produced — two independent accounts of the same session, compared.

The premise has evidence from this session: an adversarial reviewer with no conversational context
returned 21 findings, three of which would have broken the next session. A reviewer that reads the
raw transcript rather than the participant's summary is a stronger version of the same idea, because
the participant's record inherits the participant's blind spots. Two records disagreeing is itself
the signal.

Composes with `000003`, the mid-session notes skill — use both, then diff the accounts.

**Incremental extraction.** A deterministic script to extract the transcript, and a diff between the
current extract and the previous one, so each pass analyses only what is new rather than re-reading
the whole file. Transcripts are large and grow monotonically, so re-analysing from the top gets
expensive fast and produces mostly the same conclusions.

Worth deciding: what the extract format is and whether it is committed or ephemeral; where the
previous extract is stored for diffing; whether the reviewing agent sees the working agent's record
before writing its own, or only afterward — seeing it first risks anchoring, seeing it after costs a
pass; and what happens when the two records disagree on a fact rather than an emphasis.

Related: `000007`, which triages ideas rather than sessions but is the same shape — an independent
pass over a record the primary worker produced.

title: Ideation dashboard
body:
An HTML page for working the idea system end to end. Name to be improved.

- **Input field** wired to an idea-manager agent that accepts an idea, documents it into
  `ideas.md`, and starts triage and review without a session being open.
- **Idea browser** — read, filter and navigate entries by status, date, area.
- **Idea metrics** — actualisation rate, fizzle rate (discarded), duplication rate,
  investigated-to-promoted ratios.

Capture without a session is the part that changes behaviour most: right now an idea only gets
recorded if a session happens to be running, which silently filters for ideas that occur at a
keyboard.

Overlaps `000007` (the triage agent this would front) and `000008` (the metrics it would render) —
recorded separately because a dashboard is a different artifact from either, and could be built on
top of both or ahead of them.

Related: [PLAN-003](../01-plans/PLAN-003-dynamic-html-generation/PLAN-003-overview.md) and
`sys-html`, which is the framework this would be the first real consumer of — worth noting, since
`PROMPT-003` asks whether the projection and the HTML layer have any consumer yet. This would be one.

title: A backlog review and re-prioritisation recipe
body:
`/backlog` stops with a placeholder when nothing is ready — meaning everything is blocked, complete
or deferred — and says a review is needed without saying how to do one. That gap is deliberate:
defining a prioritisation process before it has ever been needed is building ahead of demand, and the
backlog currently holds 88 phases so the case is not close.

Worth defining when it becomes real: what triggers a review beyond an empty ready-set; how `next_up`
is rebuilt and by whom; whether deferred phases are reconsidered on a schedule or only on evidence;
what un-defers a phase whose gate cannot be met by waiting — `phase-mem-15` through `-19` gate on
recorded retrieval failures that nothing currently records; and whether the review is a session type
under `phase-ses-01` or a command.

Related: `phase-gov-03`, which reviews system complexity and will likely touch prioritisation anyway.

title: Skip the test preflight when the tree is provably clean
body:
`/backlog` runs governance and the full suite before orienting. At 266 tests in under two seconds
that is free. It will not stay free.

Once the suite is slow enough to notice, and once there is a remote with CI gates and a required PR
before promotion to `dev`, a clean tree at a commit CI already validated has been tested — re-running
locally proves nothing new. The preflight could then check provenance instead of re-executing:
working tree clean, HEAD matches a commit with a green CI result, no untracked files that would
change behaviour.

Worth deciding then: what counts as proof a commit was validated; whether governance still always
runs, since it is fast and catches document drift the tests do not; and whether the skip is automatic
or an explicit flag, because a preflight that silently decides not to check is worse than one that
takes ten seconds.

Blocked on infrastructure that does not exist — there is no remote until `phase-priv-05`.

title: Investigate other useful commands
body:
`/backlog` is the first command in this repository and it exists because a repeated manual routine
was worth encoding. Others probably qualify. Worth finding them rather than waiting to notice.

Candidates observed as repeated routines during this session:

- **Close a session** — `OPS-001` documents the procedure in prose precisely because closing was
  being done from memory each time. That is the strongest candidate.
- **Allocate a code and stub a document** — `--next-code`, then write front matter by hand, then
  regenerate the catalog. Mechanical and easy to get subtly wrong.
- **Verify** — governance, tests, catalog regeneration and link checking, run together. Done perhaps
  fifteen times today by hand.
- **Adversarial review** — spawning a reviewer with no conversational context, which found three
  session-breaking defects when finally run. Valuable enough that it should not depend on remembering
  to ask.
- **Park an idea** — superseded by the tool in `phase-idea-01`, but the command surface is a separate
  question from the writer.

The test for each: is it a routine done from memory, where doing it slightly differently each time
causes real problems? That is what `OPS-001` says about session closing, and it is the same reason
`/backlog` exists.

Worth deciding: which are commands versus skills — a command for anything that mutates or claims,
per the reasoning in the eleventh amendment of `SESS-2026-09-06-08`; whether they compose or
duplicate; and whether they belong in this repository or in the portable set that `phase-tool-02`
would generalise.

title: Investigate hooks for the repository and audit settings.json
body:
Claude Code supports **hooks** — commands the harness runs automatically at defined points (before or after a tool call, on session start, on stop). Nothing in this repository uses them, so every standing rule is currently enforced by an agent remembering to follow it.

That is worth investigating precisely because this session produced an example of the failure: `dev` was left red for three commits because `--catalog` prints rather than writes and the regeneration was redirected away. A hook running the governance check on stop would have caught it immediately. `PLAN-008` raises the same question in the abstract — whether the closing protocol should be enforced by a check rather than a written procedure, since a documented step that is skipped leaves no trace while a check that fails does.

Worth deciding when it becomes real:

- **Which rules deserve a hook rather than a sentence.** Candidates: the governance check before a session ends, catalog staleness, the no-remote push gate (a hook could make `git remote add` impossible rather than merely forbidden), and `_private/` reads.
- **Where the boundary sits between a hook and a test.** A test catches drift at CI time; a hook catches it at the moment it happens. Both, for the same rule, may be one too many.
- **Whether hooks are tool-specific in a way that breaks AGENTS.md's promise.** AGENTS.md is written for any agent, not only Claude Code, and hooks live in `.claude/settings.json`. The same tension PLAN-008 records as an open question about where entry points belong.

**Audit `settings.json` as part of this.** `.claude/settings.local.json` is the only settings file present, it is untracked personal configuration, and nobody has reviewed what it permits. The audit should establish what is set today, what belongs in tracked project settings rather than local settings, and whether any permission is broader than the work requires.

Related: `PLAN-008` (session lifecycle protocols) and its open question on enforcement; idea `000012` on skipping the test preflight, which is the same question about where automation should sit.

title: X content series documenting d-system development
body:
Generate a growing sequence of posts for X (Twitter) that document what we're building with d-system. The intent is to build in public and share progress, decisions, and learnings as the system develops.

This would be a curated content calendar that pulls from:
- Architecture decisions (ADRs)
- Completed phases and their outcomes
- Technical insights and lessons learned
- Project milestones and shipped features

The sequence should grow over time as more work completes, creating a narrative arc from initial concept through current state.

Unresolved: format/length for X posts, frequency, which aspects to prioritize for public sharing given confidentiality considerations, how to automate generation vs. manual curation.

title: Multi-platform public presence strategy in AI space
body:
Explore multiple social media and professional platforms to build public visibility and credibility in the AI space. This goes beyond just X — could include LinkedIn, Bluesky, GitHub, Mastodon, or other emerging platforms.

The idea combines three things:
1. Platform strategy: which platforms align with audience and goals? Where is the AI community most engaged? Which platforms support the kind of content we want to share?
2. Content strategy: what narrative makes sense across platforms? How does it differ by platform? What's the posting cadence and format for each?
3. Actual content: start producing and scheduling posts, threads, technical breakdowns, and essays that showcase expertise and the d-system work.

Related to 000015 (X content series) but broader — 000015 is about one platform and one narrative thread, this explores the full ecosystem. Could inform decisions about audience positioning, whether building in public on d-system should be the anchor or one spoke of a larger presence, and how to balance multiple streams without burnout.

Unresolved: which platforms are worth the effort, whether to build presence first then anchor to d-system or vice versa, whether to maintain separate personas or unified voice, content production cadence, measurement of success.

title: AI-powered content automation pipeline for social media
body:
Use AI agents and automation to generate, curate, and schedule content across multiple platforms, directly supporting the multi-platform presence strategy (000016) while addressing burnout concerns.

The system should:
- Automatically generate draft posts from d-system work (architecture decisions, completed phases, technical insights)
- Adapt content to platform-specific formats and audiences (X thread, LinkedIn post, technical essay, etc.)
- Schedule posts with optimal timing for each platform
- Track engagement and feedback to inform future content
- Reduce manual overhead to sustainable levels

This directly validates d-system's core purpose: using AI to automate work overhead. The system becomes both a showcase of what d-system can do (eating its own dog food) and a practical tool for maintaining public presence without constant manual effort.

Unresolved: which content sources to prioritize, how much human review/approval is needed, how to ensure quality/brand consistency, what metrics matter for success, whether to build this as a feature of d-system itself or a separate tool.

title: Tagging and plan-mapping system for ideas
body:
Enhance the idea tracking system with the ability to retroactively tag ideas and map them to plans when they are adopted or promoted.

Current state: ideas are recorded, can be marked as promoted with --promoted-to PLAN-NNN, but there is no way to:
- Add tags to ideas for discovery and organization
- Search or filter ideas by tag
- See the relationship between an idea and the plan(s) it influenced
- Track which ideas contributed to a given plan (reverse mapping)

This would include:
- A tagging component in the JSONL schema (tags array on each idea record)
- Ability to add tags retroactively via tools/append_idea.py
- A tag vocabulary/registry (like tags.json for projects/commitments)
- Generation of a tagged index in ideas.md
- Queries: "which ideas are tagged X", "which ideas fed into PLAN-016", "show me all open ideas tagged as platform-strategy"

This would make the idea list discoverable and connectable to the planning system — right now promoted ideas disappear into plans with no trace back to what sparked them. Overlap detection (ADR-010) would also be easier with proper tagging.

Unresolved: tag vocabulary (should it be defined upfront or grow organically?), whether to track which plan version an idea was promoted into, how to handle ideas that influence multiple plans.

title: Extend idea schema with Notes, Review, and Linkage
body:
Enhance the append-only idea event log to support retroactive annotation, agent review feedback, and linking between ideas.

**Current problem:** Once an idea is created, the only thing that changes is its status. There's no way to:
- Add notes or commentary to an existing idea
- Record agent review findings attached to an idea
- Link ideas that are related (extended from, superseded by, duplicates of, etc.)
- Track which ideas informed or were informed by others

**Proposed additions:**

1. **Notes field** — new event type 'annotated' that appends a timestamped note to an idea. Multiple notes for the same idea accumulate in order. Example: agent adds a note during review, owner adds context, triage agent finds related work.

2. **Agent Review Notes** — similar to Notes but semantically distinct. New event type 'reviewed' or notes tagged with source='agent'. Carries the reviewer's findings without overwriting the idea itself.

3. **Linked To / Extended From** — new event type 'linked' that references another idea. Could carry a relationship type (duplicates, supersedes, extends, related-to, inspired-by, etc.). An idea can have multiple links.

4. **Superseded status** — currently ideas can be promoted or discarded. A third terminal state 'superseded' (optionally with a link to the idea that superseded it) would handle the case where an old idea is replaced by a newer one. Or it could be a link type rather than a status.

**Implementation notes:**

- Each new field type requires a new event type in the schema
- The fold() function in append_idea.py must know how to aggregate these events back into the idea's current state
  - Notes: collect into an array
  - Agent Review Notes: collect into an array (or merge into Notes with metadata about source)
  - Links: collect into an array
  - Superseded: record the link and mark as terminal
- New tools needed in append_idea.py: , ,  (or similar commands)
- generate_ideas_md.py would need to render these new fields in the markdown output
- The fold() function's output format would change (add notes, reviews, links to each idea state)

**Unresolved:**
- Should notes and reviews be separate fields or unified with metadata?
- What link types should be predefined vs. open-ended?
- Should 'superseded' be a status or a link type?
- When rendering ideas.md, how verbose should the new fields be? Show all notes or just count/summary?
- Should there be a command to bulk-link ideas (e.g., retroactively mark 000016 and 000015 as related)?
- How should the schema's transition table be updated to allow status transitions for ideas with new fields?

title: MCP-mediated multi-agent coordination with a Librarian context service
body:
Build an MCP server as the single source of truth for multi-agent coordination in this repo, replacing direct file reads with a mediated protocol. Concretely:

- An MCP server that agents talk to instead of reading docs/backlog/claims files directly. It becomes the authoritative interface for documentation, file/phase claims, and worktree checkouts across concurrent agents — resolving what today is done by hand (editing backlog.yaml claims, running governance to check collisions, manually setting up git worktrees per AGENTS.md's concurrent-agent protocol).
- A vector database behind the MCP server, holding indexed context (decisions, session history, plan/requirement content) so agents can query semantically instead of grepping/reading whole files.
- A "Librarian" agent (possibly multiple librarians plus a "library manager" coordinating them) that scans developer/agent sessions and plan documents to extract, summarize, catalog and cross-reference decisions and context — essentially automating what session records and governance memories do manually today.
- The Librarian rebuilds/curates small, targeted context bundles for ephemeral short-lived agent batches, so each agent gets only the slice of context it needs rather than loading full documents — a context-window optimization, MemGPT-style (tiered/managed memory rather than a flat context window).
- A pub/sub channel from the Librarian (or the owner via the Librarian) that can act as a kill-switch — signal a running agent to stop when it's off track, or pause agents to resolve a collision (e.g. two agents about to conflict on the same files/systems) and patch their context before resuming.

Motivation: today's coordination is entirely file-based (docs/09-backlog/backlog.yaml as the lock table, `uv run python -m src.governance` as the lock check, manual git worktrees per AGENTS.md) and works, but is manual, per-session, and doesn't scale context efficiently as more concurrent agents and longer session histories accumulate — this session alone involved a real cross-agent deliverable-path collision and two duplicate-code collisions that had to be resolved by hand. This idea proposes making that coordination live behind a queryable service instead of being re-derived by each agent reading raw files every time.

Open questions: how this relates to the existing file-based governance system (replaces it vs. sits alongside it as an accelerator that still treats backlog.yaml/git as ground truth), what "off track" detection would actually look like for the kill-switch, whether a vector DB is the right retrieval mechanism versus the existing DuckDB projection, and how Librarian-authored summaries would themselves be governed/audited so they don't silently drift from the source documents they summarize.

title: No backup or disaster-recovery plan for a repository that is deliberately unpushed
body:
This idea came out of an owner-directed research task: two agents were asked to independently read the existing ideas, plans, and repo state and propose new topics worth investigating; this is one of ten proposed by one of them (the second agent hit a session limit before returning results).

AGENTS.md forbids adding a remote until PLAN-006's phase-priv-05 (the confidentiality sweep) completes, and .gitignore permanently excludes _private/ from git entirely. That means the entire commit history of this repository, plus anything ever written to _private/, currently exists in exactly one place: this machine's disk. PLAN-006 is about what becomes safe to publish, not about surviving a disk failure in the meantime — it explicitly gates publishing, not building. Nothing addresses what happens if the single local copy is lost before the sweep completes, and _private/'s permanent exclusion from git means a future remote would never cover it anyway.

What it would touch: probably a new governance document or an addition to AGENTS.md/GOV-001 describing the accepted backup posture, and possibly a small tool if an encrypted local/off-machine copy mechanism is chosen.

What's unresolved: whether "backup" means an encrypted off-machine copy, a second local disk, or a documented decision to accept the risk until the confidentiality sweep lands — and separately, whether _private/'s blanket git-exclusion is itself worth revisiting in favor of a lighter-weight local-only backup mechanism that doesn't require it to ever reach a remote.

title: People and commitments have zero real records despite being the system's stated core purpose
body:
This idea came out of an owner-directed research task: two agents were asked to independently read the existing ideas, plans, and repo state and propose new topics worth investigating; this is one of ten proposed by one of them (the second agent hit a session limit before returning results).

_data/people/ and _data/commitments/ each contain only a .gitkeep. ARCH-002 recorded this as of 2026-09-05 ("0 people... 0 commitments, 0 tasks") and it is still true today. CLAUDE.md states the project's purpose as "tracking people, projects, commitments, and tasks," yet 33 populated _data/projects/*.json files exist against zero commitments or people — the schema and DDL are complete for all four entities, but only one of them is actually in use.

Worth investigating directly: is this because the owner genuinely has no open commitments worth tracking right now, or because there's no low-friction way to create one — unlike ideas, which got a dedicated append-only writer (tools/append_idea.py) specifically because hand-editing JSON was friction that caused a real corruption incident (idea 000019). PLAN-006 phase 3 mentions seeding "at least one person and one commitment with tasks," but only into the fictional public example set, not as a fix for real usage.

What it would touch: possibly a writer/CLI for people and commitments analogous to tools/append_idea.py, or simply a conversation with the owner about whether commitments genuinely don't exist right now versus the tooling being the blocker.

What's unresolved: which of the two explanations is actually true, and if it's friction, what the minimum viable writer would look like given commitments (unlike ideas) reference other entities (project_id, promoted_to people) rather than being a flat append-only log.

title: _tmpagent/'s claim protocol has no entry in the systems.yaml maturity registry
body:
This idea came out of an owner-directed research task: two agents were asked to independently read the existing ideas, plans, and repo state and propose new topics worth investigating; this is one of ten proposed by one of them (the second agent hit a session limit before returning results).

_tmpagent/AGENTS.md and _tmpagent/claims.jsonl define a real, active protocol — claim, activate, release — for files agents in sibling worktrees must read, and AGENTS.md treats it as load-bearing enough to dedicate a full paragraph to it under "Key conventions." But docs/08-governance/systems.yaml (the maturity/component registry that `--inventory` reads) has no sys-tmpagent or equivalent entry alongside sys-backlog, sys-portfolio, and the rest. Every other tracked mechanism with a real lifecycle — ideas, backlog, document codes — got a system entry; this one didn't, so the registry that's supposed to answer "what exists and how mature is it" is silently blind to a mechanism this very session used repeatedly.

What it would touch: docs/08-governance/systems.yaml (add an entry), possibly a one-line cross-reference from AGENTS.md's existing paragraph.

What's unresolved: whether this is a plain oversight or a deliberate choice — that _tmpagent/ is infrastructure-for-infrastructure and doesn't warrant registry status — because that reasoning isn't written down anywhere either way. Worth a quick decision rather than a full investigation.

title: Four entity schemas are validated in the pipeline with no DDL table, no data directory, and no CLAUDE.md mention
body:
This idea came out of an owner-directed research task: two agents were asked to independently read the existing ideas, plans, and repo state and propose new topics worth investigating; this is one of ten proposed by one of them (the second agent hit a session limit before returning results).

src/db/source_validation.py's ENTITY_DIRECTORIES maps interactions→interaction, decisions→decision, waiting-on→waiting-on, and development-events→development-event, each backed by a real schema file in schemas/. But sql/001_schema.sql has no interactions, decisions, waiting_on, or development_events tables (confirmed by grepping every CREATE TABLE), no corresponding _data/ subdirectory exists for any of them, and CLAUDE.md's "Data Architecture" section documents only the original four entities (project/person/commitment/tag) — none of these four. They belong to the planned capture system (PLAN-007/PLAN-009, sys-capture: planned), so the overall plan is known, but this specific three-way drift pattern — schema shipped and wired into validation, DDL and data directory absent, orienting documentation silent — is worth naming as its own finding: schemas are landing ahead of the documentation a reader relies on to know what actually exists.

What it would touch: sql/001_schema.sql (add the four tables when the capture plan actually implements them, or explicitly defer), CLAUDE.md's Data Architecture section (at minimum, a note that these four are schema-only/pending), and possibly tools/rebuild_db.py once tables exist.

What's unresolved: whether to treat this as "wait for PLAN-007/009 to land the DDL properly" or as a smaller near-term fix — adding a one-line "schema exists, not yet backed by a table" note to CLAUDE.md and systems.yaml so the drift is at least visible in the meantime.

title: No recovery procedure exists for an abandoned agent claim in the concurrency protocol
body:
This idea came out of an owner-directed research task: two agents were asked to independently read the existing ideas, plans, and repo state and propose new topics worth investigating; this is one of ten proposed by one of them (the second agent hit a session limit before returning results).

AGENTS.md's "Concurrent agents" sections cover claiming a phase, working in a worktree, completing and handing off, and resolving collisions (backlog.yaml conflicts, duplicate codes, source conflicts, a red rebase) — but nothing covers what happens when an agent claims a phase (status: active, agent: agent-<name>), starts a worktree, and then simply stops mid-session — a crash, a timeout, a context exhaustion, an API session limit like the one that just ended one of the two agents that produced this very batch of ideas — without releasing the claim or completing the hand-off. The phase stays active indefinitely, the worktree and branch sit orphaned at ../d-system-worktrees/<phase-id>, and no other agent may claim overlapping systems because the Conflicts column will keep showing the dead claim as live.

What it would touch: AGENTS.md's concurrency section (a new "recovering an abandoned claim" procedure), possibly src/governance/backlog.py (a staleness signal — an `updated` timestamp that hasn't moved in N sessions, or a check for a worktree directory with no corresponding live process) and GOV-003 (recording the accepted recovery decision).

What's unresolved: what actually signals a claim is abandoned versus just long-running, who is allowed to release someone else's claim (the owner only, or any agent that can show the worktree is gone), and whether this should be a governance check that flags stale claims for the owner to review, or a fully manual owner action with a documented procedure.

title: CI only compiles the frontend — no test runner or lint gate exists for ts/
body:
This idea came out of an owner-directed research task: two agents were asked to independently read the existing ideas, plans, and repo state and propose new topics worth investigating; this is one of ten proposed by one of them (the second agent hit a session limit before returning results).

.github/workflows/ci.yaml's frontend job runs `npm ci` and `npm run build` and nothing else: no eslint config exists anywhere under ts/, and no test runner (no vitest, no jest) is configured in ts/package.json. ARCH-003 already flags browser-behavior gaps for the planned HTML feature specifically, but the underlying gap is broader and predates that plan — even the current two-file scaffold (App.tsx, main.tsx) has zero behavioral verification, only a TypeScript compile check.

What it would touch: ts/package.json (add vitest or similar, add eslint config), .github/workflows/ci.yaml (add the new steps to the frontend job).

What's unresolved: which test runner/lint config to standardize on, and whether to set this up now while the frontend is a two-file scaffold (cheap) or wait until the HTML generation feature actually starts building real components (when retrofitting would be more expensive, but so is maintaining infrastructure for code that doesn't exist yet). Worth deciding before the HTML work begins in earnest, per ARCH-003's own recommendation to fix backend gaps before that work starts.

title: No mechanical check that a completed phase's actual diff stayed inside its declared systems/deliverables
body:
This idea came out of an owner-directed research task: two agents were asked to independently read the existing ideas, plans, and repo state and propose new topics worth investigating; this is one of ten proposed by one of them (the second agent hit a session limit before returning results).

src/governance/backlog.py's collision-checking compares declared deliverable paths between phases before work starts — that's how two concurrent agents avoid claiming overlapping work, and it caught a real false collision this session (two phases both declaring the bare .claude directory). But AGENTS.md's instruction to "stay inside your phase's declared systems and deliverables... if the work genuinely requires a file outside them, stop" is enforced only by an agent choosing to follow it; nothing diffs a phase's actual `git diff <range>` against its declared paths after the fact. The "resolve collisions" section confirms this indirectly: a stray-file violation is only ever caught when it collides with a peer's simultaneous claim and produces a merge conflict — a solo agent drifting outside its declarations with no peer working nearby would never be caught by anything mechanical.

This session's own session-close command already has a sub-agent independently review a phase's diff against its acceptance conditions before allowing completion — the same review already reads the diff, so declared-path containment is a natural, cheap addition to check at the same point, or alternatively a small standalone governance check that greps `git diff --stat` against `deliverables`.

What it would touch: .claude/commands/session-close.md (add containment to the sub-agent review's checklist) and/or src/governance/backlog.py (a new mechanical check).

What's unresolved: whether this belongs in the human/agent-judgment review step (session-close) or as an automated, hard-fail governance check — the latter is stronger but needs a rule for legitimate incidental touches (e.g. catalog.md, which almost every phase regenerates regardless of its declared deliverables).

title: External trigger gateway for agent workflows outside chat sessions
body:
This idea comes from a second, independent two-agent research pass (mirroring the one that produced ideas 000021-000027), staged first as ungoverned notes under docs/00-working/ per ADR-010, then reviewed and deduplicated before being recorded. The source material described this both as a combined idea (gateway + a durable run ledger together) and as two separable pieces "so trigger intake, run durability and process supervision can be evaluated independently" — this entry keeps only the gateway half; the ledger is recorded separately (see the idea about a durable agent workflow run ledger) so each concept is independently promotable.

Create a local trigger gateway that accepts filesystem, scheduled/cron, webhook and CLI events and normalizes each into a deduplicated event carrying its source, payload hash, received time and requested workflow — the ingress boundary for operating this system between chat sessions rather than only ever being invoked from one. This fills a real gap: the repository has owner-invoked commands and planned agent workflows, but no external trigger protocol at all today. It's deliberately provider-neutral and separate from the execution/durability layer, so trigger adapters can be evaluated and swapped independently of how runs are persisted.

Touches: new trigger/job intake modules, an event-normalization layer, and whatever queue or hand-off mechanism feeds the durable run ledger.

Verification: submit one fixture event through each adapter (filesystem, cron, webhook, CLI), restart the gateway, replay a duplicate delivery, and prove one logical trigger produces exactly one queued run carrying its original payload hash.

What's unresolved: how this relates to the MCP/Librarian coordination idea already recorded (000020) — that idea is about context and memory curation across agents; this one is about triggering and admitting work in the first place. They're complementary, not the same thing, but the boundary between "gateway decides a run should start" and "Librarian decides what context that run gets" needs a real design pass before either is built.

title: Durable agent workflow run ledger with resumable steps
body:
This idea comes from a second, independent two-agent research pass (mirroring the one that produced ideas 000021-000027), staged first as ungoverned notes under docs/00-working/ per ADR-010, then reviewed and deduplicated before being recorded. Split out from a combined "gateway + ledger" framing in the source material into its own entry, alongside the external trigger gateway idea, so the two can be evaluated independently.

Persist every agent workflow run with a correlation ID, the triggering payload's hash, the model/tool versions used, a context-pack hash, its budget, timeout, retry count, checkpoints, produced artifacts and final disposition. A run must be able to resume after an interruption — a crash, a timeout, a session limit like the one that actually ended one of this session's own brainstorming agents mid-task — without repeating completed side effects. This is the durability layer the repository's agent workflows don't have today: work either finishes in one conversation or its partial progress is lost.

Touches: new run/step/checkpoint tables (likely DuckDB), an execution adapter kept provider-neutral so it doesn't hard-code a specific model or tool, and whatever surfaces run status (API route, small UI, or just a CLI query for now).

Verification: interrupt a multi-step fixture run after step two, restart the worker, and prove steps one and two are not repeated while step three completes exactly once. Also verify idempotent delivery and timeout/retry behavior end to end, and that cancellation actually stops further side effects rather than just marking a row cancelled.

What's unresolved: whether this needs its own storage or can live inside the existing DuckDB projection alongside everything else, and how much of this is worth building before there's a second real trigger-driven workflow to prove it against — a durability layer with one caller is hard to validate.

title: Always-on worker host and watchdog for supervised agent runs
body:
This idea comes from a second, independent two-agent research pass (mirroring the one that produced ideas 000021-000027), staged first as ungoverned notes under docs/00-working/ per ADR-010, then reviewed and deduplicated before being recorded. It's the third of three related pieces (alongside the external trigger gateway and the durable run ledger ideas), kept deliberately separate so the system can run in one-shot, scheduled, or continuously-supervised modes without process supervision being a hard requirement for the other two.

Add a small supervised worker process that drains queued runs, enforces concurrency limits and quiet hours, heartbeats its own progress, and marks work as abandoned for review when a heartbeat goes stale — rather than silently retrying a run whose side effects might already be half-applied. This only makes sense once the trigger gateway and run ledger ideas above exist; on its own it's a scheduling daemon with nothing to schedule.

Touches: a new supervised worker/daemon process, heartbeat and quiet-hours configuration, and a review surface for abandoned runs.

Verification: kill and restart the worker and confirm queued work resumes correctly; test quiet-hour deferral; force a run past its timeout and confirm it's flagged rather than silently retried; confirm a stale heartbeat surfaces for owner review instead of being auto-resolved.

What's unresolved: everything about priority and sequencing — this is explicitly the least urgent of the three related ideas, since it has no purpose until the gateway and ledger exist and are actually being used for something.

title: Capability and approval broker for agent actions
body:
This idea comes from a second, independent two-agent research pass (mirroring the one that produced ideas 000021-000027), staged first as ungoverned notes under docs/00-working/ per ADR-010, then reviewed and deduplicated before being recorded.

Give every agent run an explicit, narrow capability set — read-only repository access, source mutation, external network, publication, or other specifically named actions — and route anything sensitive through an approval request carrying its scope, reason, expiry and an immutable decision record. Denied capabilities need to be enforced at the actual tool boundary, not just described in a prompt an agent could ignore or misread. This repository already governs documents and phase claims (the backlog lock table, the concurrency protocol this very session used extensively), but nothing today authorizes what an agent is allowed to *do* at runtime — that gap is exactly what would need closing before any trigger-driven work (see the external trigger gateway idea) could safely run unattended between chat sessions, where there's no human in the loop to notice an agent doing something it shouldn't.

Touches: new capability/approval schemas, a tool-execution boundary that actually enforces them (not just a convention), an audit record of every decision, and some review surface for pending approvals.

Verification: test allow, deny and escalation paths directly; prove a denied action genuinely cannot mutate a source file or reach the network (not just that it's discouraged); confirm approvals expire and are properly scoped; replay the audit trail and confirm it can explain every attempted action, not just the successful ones.

What's unresolved: how this relates to the existing AGENTS.md concurrency protocol and the confidentiality/push-gate rules already in force — those are today enforced by an agent choosing to follow written instructions, which is exactly the weaker guarantee this idea proposes to replace with something mechanical. Also related to idea 000020 (the MCP/Librarian coordination proposal), which includes a "kill-switch" concept — this idea's approval/capability boundary and that one's pause/kill mechanism are complementary controls, not the same thing, and would need to be designed together rather than separately if both are pursued.

title: Evidence-backed provenance graph for memories, reports and recommendations
body:
This idea comes from a second, independent two-agent research pass (mirroring the one that produced ideas 000021-000027), staged first as ungoverned notes under docs/00-working/ per ADR-010, then reviewed and deduplicated before being recorded. It unifies what the two source agents separately proposed as a "provenance manifest" and a "claim registry" into one idea, since both are really the same underlying capability viewed from different angles.

Record the sources behind every memory, recommendation, generated report, context pack and dashboard metric: the source file/event and its anchor, the query or prompt that produced it, the model/tool version involved, any human decision made about it, and the derived artifact itself. Make the resulting graph queryable in both directions — "why does this claim exist?" and "what outputs need reconsidering if this source changes?" Today, evidence fields and memory confidence are local, per-record concepts, and generated outputs (reports, rendered views) have no end-to-end lineage back to what produced them. This would also help distinguish a captured fact from a derived interpretation from a recommendation, without changing the append-only nature of the underlying source records.

Touches: evidence/claim metadata on memories and other records, new DuckDB provenance tables, the rebuild/generation tooling (tools/rebuild_db.py and report generators), retrieval, and any detail views that would surface "why is this here."

Verification: generate a fixture artifact and assert its complete dependency graph is captured; modify one source and confirm only the genuinely affected outputs are identified as needing reconsideration; confirm provenance survives a full rebuild; confirm a contradictory or stale claim surfaces rather than silently disappearing.

What's unresolved: how much of this can be retrofitted onto the existing brain/ memory system versus needing to be designed in from the start for the still-largely-unbuilt reporting/HTML-generation features, and whether the scope should start much smaller (just idea/plan lineage, which already has an append-only event log to build on) before attempting the full cross-system version.

title: Temporal projection explorer for idea/plan/portfolio history
body:
This idea comes from a second, independent two-agent research pass (mirroring the one that produced ideas 000021-000027), staged first as ungoverned notes under docs/00-working/ per ADR-010, then reviewed and deduplicated before being recorded.

Expose deterministic "as of" snapshots and two-point diffs over ideas, plans and portfolio entities: show which status, annotation, relationship, promotion or plan-phase fact changed, when it became known, and which source event supports that fact. The repository is already investing heavily in immutable event histories and derived projections — the idea log's whole design (idea 000004's amendment/fold work, this session's own fold() consolidation) exists specifically so that "what did we believe on date D" is answerable by replaying to D — but nothing today actually consumes that capability; every current view shows only present state. A temporal explorer would turn retained history into something actually usable, and would force the time-axis definitions already discussed in the idea/plan lifecycle architecture (PLAN-017) to become genuinely testable rather than theoretical.

Touches: the replay/query layer (likely building on src/db/ideas.py's fold() and whatever the plan-lifecycle work produces), new DuckDB views for "as of" queries, and eventually API routes and a frontend view — though a CLI-only version would already prove the concept.

Verification: fixture histories produce stable, repeatable snapshots immediately before and after a state-change boundary; diffs identify exactly the fields that changed and nothing else; an amendment's timestamp never masquerades as the original event's timestamp; an invalid or ambiguous history is reported as such rather than silently reordered into something that looks clean.

What's unresolved: this depends on the idea/plan lifecycle work (PLAN-017, and phase-idea-07's identity/amendment fold specifically) actually landing first — there's currently only one idea with more than a `created` event in the real log, so this has nothing real to query yet. Worth revisiting once phase-idea-07 completes.

title: Portfolio scenario simulator for what-if planning
body:
This idea comes from a second, independent two-agent research pass (mirroring the one that produced ideas 000021-000027), staged first as ungoverned notes under docs/00-working/ per ADR-010, then reviewed and deduplicated before being recorded.

Add isolated what-if scenarios over the derived portfolio projection: defer a project, change available capacity, move a deadline, close a commitment, or reallocate tasks, then recompute whatever signals exist and compare the scenario against the real baseline — without ever writing to source JSON, the live database, or the idea log. The portfolio-signals work planned elsewhere in this repo describes the portfolio as it currently is; this would be a genuinely new capability rather than another signal definition, and it creates a concrete consumer for whatever the signal system eventually computes — supporting a decision before the owner commits to it, rather than only reporting on decisions already made.

Touches: a scenario input schema, an isolated projection (a copy of the relevant DuckDB tables or an in-memory equivalent, never the live one), the same signal SQL the real portfolio uses, and eventually an API route and a comparison view.

Verification: run deterministic fixtures with controlled, known changes and confirm the source data and the real baseline projection remain byte-for-byte unchanged afterward; confirm scenario isolation (two scenarios run in sequence don't leak into each other) and repeatability (same scenario, same result); confirm a discarded scenario is genuinely gone from normal views unless explicitly exported.

What's unresolved: this depends on the portfolio-signals system actually existing first (per systems.yaml, most signal work is still planned, not implemented) — there's nothing to simulate against yet. Worth revisiting once at least one real signal is computable from real data, per the earlier idea about people/commitments having zero real records.

title: Contract compiler and mutation-driven fixture suite from JSON Schema
body:
This idea comes from a second, independent two-agent research pass (mirroring the one that produced ideas 000021-000027), staged first as ungoverned notes under docs/00-working/ per ADR-010, then reviewed and deduplicated before being recorded.

Make JSON Schema the single executable contract source for Python models, TypeScript types, OpenAPI fragments, and both valid and invalid fixture factories — with deterministic generation and mutation-based checks so that schema, backend, frontend, loader and governance behavior can't silently drift apart from each other. AGENTS.md's own "Adding a domain entity" section already lists six manual steps across schemas/, sql/, tools/, src/models/ and src/api/routes/ — a process that's easy to get partway through and leave inconsistent, which is exactly the kind of drift another proposed idea in this same batch (interactions/decisions/waiting-on/development-events being schema-and-validator-only with no DDL or docs) already shows happening in practice. This is deliberately about cross-system consistency and negative-case testing, not a new runtime subsystem — it's tooling that makes the existing manual process faster and harder to get wrong.

Touches: schemas/ (as the source of truth, unchanged in shape but now consumed programmatically), a new contract-generation tool, src/models/, whatever TypeScript types the frontend eventually needs, API metadata, and generated test fixtures.

Verification: repeated generation from the same schema is byte-stable; a deliberate schema mutation produces the expected stale-artifact failure somewhere downstream; generated Python and TypeScript type checks both pass; a targeted invalid-data mutation fails at the correct validator boundary, not a generic catch-all; existing hand-authored exceptions to the pattern remain explicit rather than silently overwritten.

What's unresolved: how much of this is worth building generically versus just fixing the concrete four-entity drift it was prompted by directly — a general contract compiler is a much bigger investment than closing one specific gap, and it's not yet clear the repo has enough entity types to justify the generic version over doing it by hand a few more times.

title: Recommendation calibration loop measuring whether advice helped
body:
This idea comes from a second, independent two-agent research pass (mirroring the one that produced ideas 000021-000027), staged first as ungoverned notes under docs/00-working/ per ADR-010, then reviewed and deduplicated before being recorded.

Persist every recommendation the system produces (from planned signals, from triage agents, from anything advisory) together with its supporting evidence, the owner's actual decision about it (accept, defer, dismiss, or revise), and the later observed outcome. Produce calibration reports on top of that: which recommendations were actually useful, which created false urgency, which kept being missed or deferred, and how long outcomes typically lagged the recommendation. The repository already plans signals and idea triage, but nothing measures whether that advice actually improves the owner's work — without this, the system can accumulate persuasive-sounding automation indefinitely with zero evidence it's helping. This is distinct from a next-best-action queue (which chooses what to recommend); calibration is about evaluating whether the choices were any good after the fact.

Touches: new recommendation/decision/outcome event types, whatever signal generators eventually exist, agent-run records if the trigger/ledger ideas above are built, and some reporting surface (SQL reports at minimum, a UI eventually).

Verification: build synthetic recommendation histories with known outcomes and confirm the system correctly calculates precision, deferral rate, false-urgency rate and outcome lag against them; confirm every calculated metric traces back to immutable evidence rather than a recomputed guess; confirm an outcome that hasn't happened yet is reported as genuinely unresolved rather than counted as a miss.

What's unresolved: this is the most downstream of all the ideas in this batch — it needs recommendations to actually exist and accumulate real decisions and outcomes before there's anything to calibrate against. Worth recording now as a design constraint on how signals/recommendations get built (they should be built recording-friendly from day one) rather than something to implement soon.

title: Split backlog.yaml into active and archive files before it clogs agent context
body:
docs/09-backlog/backlog.yaml records every phase ever created and GOV-002 forbids deleting
completed history ("preserve IDs and completed evidence rather than deleting history"), so the
file only grows. As of 2026-09-08 it is already 98 phases / ~3,500 lines / ~142KB, with 26 of 98
already `complete`. The governance CLI (`--ready`, `--backlog`) filters its output, so scripted
use is unaffected, but anything that reads the raw file directly (an agent orienting via the
backlog skill, a `cat`/`Read` of the file, code review) pulls every completed phase's full record
- acceptance checks, evidence, session IDs - into context whether or not it is relevant to the
work at hand. That cost is unbounded and one-directional: it only grows as more phases complete.

Idea: split into two files. `backlog.yaml` keeps only non-terminal phases (`queued`, `active`,
`blocked`, `deferred`); a new `backlog-archive.yaml` holds `complete` and `cancelled` phases,
still preserving IDs and completion evidence exactly as GOV-002 requires - this is a location
change, not a deletion, so it does not conflict with the "preserve history" rule.

What it would touch:
- `schemas/backlog.schema.json` (or a parallel archive schema)
- `src/governance/backlog.py` - `depends_on` validation currently looks up a dependency's status
  in one in-memory dict (see lines ~129-136); it would need to load and merge both files so a
  queued phase can still confirm a moved-to-archive dependency is complete.
- `docs/08-governance/GOV-002-backlog-protocol.md` - the protocol describes backlog.yaml as the
  single execution record; it would need to describe the two-file split and the merge-on-read
  behavior.
- `docs/09-backlog/README.md` - navigation pointers.
- A one-time migration moving existing `complete`/`cancelled` entries out of backlog.yaml into
  the new archive file.

What is unresolved:
- Whether the archive should be one growing file or itself partitioned (e.g. by quarter or by
  track) - the same unbounded-growth question just one level down, though at a much smaller
  per-agent-read cost since nothing needs to load the whole archive by default.
- Whether `next_up` and the active-claims table logic need any change, or whether they are
  already scoped correctly since they only ever reference non-terminal phases.
- Interacts with idea 000006 (index-width audit) only tangentially - that idea is about numeric
  code ceilings, this one is about file size/context cost of retained history - but both were
  raised in the same conversation about the backlog's long-term shape and may be worth reviewing
  together.

Raised in conversation on 2026-09-08 while discussing whether backlog.yaml growth affects agent
context or performance. Would need a requirement document and a plan before any implementation,
per AGENTS.md's plan-before-code rule.

title: Formalize the requirements-vs-plans process and design
body:
AGENTS.md states the rule as a pair: "write a `requirement` document (observable statements with
verification methods) and a `plan` document" before implementing non-trivial work. In practice the
repository has far more plans than requirements - as of 2026-09-08 there are 18 plans
(`docs/01-plans/`) against 4 requirements (`docs/06-requirements/`), and only one of those four
(REQ-001/PLAN-005, the document-code system) is a clean paired example where the requirement
states observable, testable claims and the plan separately covers sequencing and implementation.
The other 14+ plans fold acceptance criteria directly into the plan document and have no
standalone requirement at all.

This came up because a conversation asked "how are requirements and plans distinguished" and the
honest answer, after reading REQ-001 and its README, was: by convention/example only. Nothing in
AGENTS.md, GOV-002, or the two directory READMEs spells out:
- When a requirement document is mandatory versus when a plan's own acceptance section suffices
  (is "non-trivial" the only gate, and if so, how is that judged in practice - several of the
  plans-only changes don't look obviously more trivial than the ones with paired requirements)
- What a requirement document must NOT contain (implementation detail, sequencing, file lists)
  versus what belongs only in the plan
- Whether a plan is allowed to exist without a requirement permanently, or whether the 14 unpaired
  plans represent a backfill obligation
- How the two document kinds' governed front matter should reference each other beyond the
  informal prose link seen in REQ-001 ("implementation plan describes how and when")

Idea: write this up as its own requirement + plan (or a single governance-track plan, consistent
with how much of the existing backlog already skips the pair) that:
1. States the actual decision rule for when a requirement document is required
2. Defines the minimal contract of a requirement document (e.g., must be pure observable/testable
   statements, no implementation detail) versus a plan
3. Decides whether the 14 requirement-less plans need to be backfilled with requirements
   retroactively, or are grandfathered
4. Updates `docs/06-requirements/README.md` and `docs/01-plans/README.md` (and AGENTS.md's
   "Plan before implementing" section) to state the rule explicitly instead of leaving it to be
   inferred from one example pair

What is unresolved: whether this itself needs a requirement document to satisfy the rule it is
about to write down (a bit self-referential) - probably fine to treat as the plan that defines the
rule rather than needing to precede itself.

Raised in the same 2026-09-08 conversation as idea about splitting backlog.yaml into an active and
archive file - unrelated topics, both surfaced while discussing longer-term shape of the
governance documentation system.

title: A priority queue for open ideas, mirroring backlog.yaml's next_up
body:
`_data/ideas.jsonl` is an append-only event log (schemas/idea.schema.json) with a `status` field
only - `open` -> `triaged` -> `reviewing` -> `promoted`/`discarded` - and no ordering concept at
all. An idea cannot enter docs/09-backlog/backlog.yaml's priority queue until it has a plan (the
backlog only tracks phases, and phases require a plan document to exist first), so between
"recorded" and "has a plan" there is currently no answer to "which open idea should be looked at
next" except reading the whole list in docs/00-working/ideas.md top to bottom.

Idea: add a small ordered list of idea IDs, living outside the append-only log, that names which
open/triaged ideas should be looked at first - the same pattern backlog.yaml already uses for
`next_up` (a plain ordered list, "everything else falls back to priority then ID"). This should
not require any change to the append-only idea schema or its legal status transitions; it is a
separate pointer structure, analogous to how backlog.yaml's next_up sits beside (not inside) each
phase's own record.

What it would likely touch:
- A new small file or field (e.g. an idea-priority list alongside docs/00-working/ideas.md, or a
  section read by tools/generate_ideas_md.py) holding the ordered list.
- tools/generate_ideas_md.py, to render the priority order in the generated markdown view (mirrors
  how the governance CLI's --ready report renders backlog next_up).
- Possibly tools/append_idea.py or a sibling script, if reordering should be a tracked operation
  rather than a hand-edited file - open question, see below.
- docs/06-requirements and docs/01-plans, since this is a design change to the idea system and
  AGENTS.md's plan-before-code rule applies.

What is unresolved:
- Whether reordering the priority list should itself be an append-only-logged operation (consistent
  with the idea system's own philosophy) or a plain mutable file like backlog.yaml's next_up,
  which is hand-edited directly today.
- Whether "priority" should just be an ordered list (mirrors next_up exactly) or whether ideas need
  a numeric priority tier the way backlog phases do (`priority: 1-4`) in addition to a jump-the-
  queue list.
- Interacts with idea 000007 (the idea triage agent, now phase-idea-02): once an agent is scouting
  and triaging ideas, a priority order would tell it (or the owner) which open ideas to triage
  first, rather than triaging in ID order.

Raised in a 2026-09-08 conversation, immediately after moving phase-idea-02 (the idea triage
agent) to the front of the backlog's next_up queue and noticing there was no equivalent mechanism
for the ideas list itself. The owner asked for this to be recorded as an idea and then written up
as a plan placed at the top of the backlog priority queue.

title: Research deterministic search algorithms across ideas, backlog, memories and decisions
body:
As the system's information surfaces grow - `_data/ideas.jsonl`, `docs/09-backlog/backlog.yaml`,
`docs/05-memories/`, ADRs/GOV/REQ/PLAN documents, session records, and eventually `_data/`'s
projects/commitments/people - an agent's ability to find the right file for a given question
degrades. Today that's handled ad hoc: grep, filename conventions, and an agent reading a README's
navigation table. That doesn't scale as volume grows (see idea `000006`, index-width audit, for the
volume side of the same trend) or as more agents work concurrently without full context of what
already exists.

Idea: research and design a family of **deterministic** search algorithms - not semantic/vector
search, which is already tracked separately as un-deferred-pending-evidence in idea `000004`
(`phase-mem-15/16/18/19`, all gated on recorded retrieval failures that nothing currently collects).
This is the deterministic half `phase-mem-18` already says comes *before* vector fallback in the
layering, but that layering has never actually been designed - only asserted as a future gate order.

Core design contract this idea is asking for:
- A set of criteria/interface that an agent must supply to a search algorithm (e.g. entity type,
  time range, status/state filters, related IDs, keyword terms, system/track tags) - a structured
  query contract, not a free-text prompt.
- Each algorithm returns a (possibly ranked) set of file paths or document/event IDs, with an
  explicit confidence or match-basis signal (exact ID match vs. tag overlap vs. keyword hit vs.
  dependency-graph proximity, etc.) so the caller knows *why* a result matched, not just that it did.
- Multiple independent deterministic algorithms should be able to run against the same query so
  their results can be cross-referenced - agreement across algorithms as a stronger relevance
  signal than any single algorithm's ranking alone.
- Final relevance judgment and the file set handed to the requesting agent stays an agent
  responsibility, not the algorithm's - the algorithms surface candidates with evidence, an agent
  (possibly a dedicated retrieval/assessment agent) filters and hands back the final set. This
  mirrors the idea system's own separation between the triage agent (`phase-idea-02`, scouts and
  attaches findings) and the owner (judges) - a deterministic search agent would scout, not decide.

Candidate deterministic techniques worth surveying rather than assuming one is sufficient:
exact ID/reference-graph traversal (depends_on, sources, systems fields already in every governed
document and backlog phase), tag/keyword indexing over frontmatter and headings, full-text/BM25-
style keyword ranking, path/naming-convention matching, temporal proximity (idea `000004`'s prior
mention of ordering-before-retrieval, and the temporal-explorer idea elsewhere in this log),
dependency/system-membership overlap, and structured field queries against the DuckDB projection
that already exists for `_data/`.

What it would touch, if pursued (research/design phase first, well before any implementation):
- Cross-cutting: `_data/ideas.jsonl`, `docs/09-backlog/backlog.yaml`, `docs/05-memories/`,
  `docs/04-decisions/`, `docs/08-governance/`, session records, and `_data/` proper.
- Likely lands in or coordinates with the `sys-memory-agents` / `sys-retrieval` systems and the
  deferred `phase-mem-*` line, but is scoped narrower than that line - deterministic only, explicitly
  not the vector/RAG work.
- Would need its own requirement + plan; this is early-stage enough that it should be scoped as
  research/survey first (idea `000038`'s req/plan formalization work may end up defining what a
  "research" plan looks like versus an "implementation" plan).

What is unresolved:
- Whether one unified query contract can serve ideas, backlog, memories and decisions, or whether
  each corpus's structure is different enough to need its own contract with a shared outer shape.
- Where the line sits between "deterministic algorithm" and "just a DuckDB query" - some of this
  may already be nearly free given the existing projection layer, which changes how much is really
  research versus assembly of what exists.
- How this interacts with the ideas-priority-queue work (`phase-idea-09`, `PLAN-019`) and the idea
  triage agent (`phase-idea-02`) - both are small, current instances of exactly the "which of these
  should I look at" problem this idea wants a general, reusable answer to.
- Relationship to `phase-mem-15/16/18/19`'s deferred status: this idea may be exactly the evidence-
  gathering or design work that unblocks un-deferring them, or it may turn out to be a fully separate
  track that only shares a system boundary.

Raised in a 2026-09-08 conversation, in the same session as the backlog-archive idea (`000037`), the
req/plan-formalization idea (`000038`), and the idea-priority-queue idea (`000039`/`PLAN-019`) -
all surfaced while discussing how the system's governance and information layers scale as volume
grows.

title: Refine the multi-agent development workflow to prevent one agent from clobbering another's uncommitted work
body:
This session hit a concrete incident: while a Claude session had uncommitted work in progress in the primary checkout (the phase-idea-09 idea-priority-queue deliverables), a concurrent Gemini agent working on phase-agnt-01 stashed and popped the other agent's uncommitted changes in order to merge its own commits into dev, without asking. This produced several artifacts of the collision that had to be cleaned up by hand: three leftover scratch scripts in the repo root (fix_conflict.py, fix_my_phase_only.py, fix_stash_conflict.py) written to patch merge/stash conflicts against a sibling worktree path, a duplicate `next_action` YAML key in docs/09-backlog/backlog.yaml left over from a bad stash-pop merge, and a session-code collision (SESS-2026-09-08-07 assigned independently by both sessions) that only surfaced when governance was rerun after the collision had already been committed to shared history.

The underlying gap: AGENTS.md's concurrent-agent protocol and GOV-003's primary-checkout exception assume agents coordinate through backlog claims (status: active, agent: field) and worktrees, but nothing currently stops one agent from running git stash against a shared primary checkout that another agent has uncommitted work sitting in, and nothing allocates session codes atomically across concurrent sessions before either lands on the shared branch. Both failures only became visible after the fact, via governance and pytest failures, rather than being prevented at the point of action.

Open questions this idea does not resolve: whether the fix is procedural (a documented rule that no agent runs `git stash`/`git pop` against the primary checkout while another agent's claim is active there) or mechanical (a lock file or check that refuses destructive git operations while a peer claim exists), and whether session-code allocation needs to move from "pick the next unused date-sequence number by inspection" to something collision-proof (e.g. reserved atomically via the same claim mechanism used for backlog phases). Also unresolved: whether this generalizes beyond Gemini specifically, or is really about any second agent operating in the same primary checkout AGENTS.md permits under the GOV-003 exception.

title: Generate an ideas & backlog HTML page for an at-a-glance view
body:
Right now the ideas queue and the backlog queue each live as their own artifact: docs/00-working/ideas.md (rendered by tools/generate_ideas_md.py from _data/ideas.jsonl and docs/00-working/ideas-priority.yaml) and docs/09-backlog/backlog.yaml (read directly, or via `uv run python -m src.governance --ready`). Both are readable, but getting a combined picture today means opening a markdown file and running a CLI report separately, and neither is glanceable the way a single page could be.

The idea is a generated HTML page — in the vein of the project's existing HTML generation framework (templates/html/, templates/styles/, tools/) — that surfaces both in one view: open ideas ranked by the priority queue (status, title, age) alongside ready/active/blocked backlog phases (priority, next_up position, plan, next_action), so a glance at one page answers "what idea or phase should I look at next" without cross-referencing two systems by hand. It would be a derived/generated artifact like ideas.md and catalog.md — never hand-edited, regenerated from _data/ideas.jsonl, docs/00-working/ideas-priority.yaml, and docs/09-backlog/backlog.yaml, and probably checked for staleness the same way `generate_ideas_md.py --check` and the catalog test already do.

Unresolved: where the generator script and its output should live (tools/ alongside the existing generate_ideas_md.py and OPS-006, versus something surfaced through the FastAPI/React app in src/ and ts/ per the project's HTML Generation Framework); whether it should be a static regenerated .html file checked into the repo (like catalog.md) or served dynamically from the DuckDB-backed API; and how much of the backlog's dependency/conflict graph (depends_on, systems, conflicts) is worth surfacing versus keeping this to a flat priority-ordered list like ideas.md already does.

title: Review documentation front matter and plan a documentation database for knowledge retrieval
body:
Every governed document in this repo (docs/01-plans, docs/04-decisions, docs/06-requirements, docs/08-governance, session records, etc.) carries YAML front matter — schema_version, id, code, kind, status, owner, created, updated, systems, depends_on — validated by src/governance and rendered flat into docs/08-governance/catalog.md. That front matter is currently only used for governance validation (uniqueness, status transitions, dependency checks) and a flat catalog listing. It is not queryable the way _data/ is queryable through DuckDB (see sql/001_schema.sql and tools/rebuild_db.py) — there is no equivalent projection for documents.

The idea is two-fold: first, an actual review pass over the front matter schema and its current field set — is it complete for what a knowledge-retrieval system would need (e.g. do session records, ADRs and plans carry enough structured metadata to be queried meaningfully — topics, related documents beyond depends_on, the systems.yaml components they touch), or does it need new fields before a retrieval system could be built on top of it. Second, planning an actual documentation database — a DuckDB projection (or similar) of every governed document's front matter and structure, parallel to how _data/ is projected into data/d_system.duckdb — so questions like "which documents touch sys-governance and are still active" or "what plans depend on doc-idea-priority-queue" can be answered by query instead of by grep or by reading docs/08-governance/catalog.md by hand.

This is the metadata/structure half of a knowledge retrieval system; it is explicitly not about the content-search half (see the companion ideas recorded alongside this one about vector DB tooling and graph DB tooling for the documentation/knowledge corpus specifically, as distinct from the existing GitNexus idea (000005) which is about code-structure graphs).
